title: Thinking Machines releases Inkling 2 Mini, a free open-weights AI model that runs on a laptop

sources.name: Thinking Machines Lab announcement (Introducing Inkling 2 Mini)

kept.claim: Thinking Machines Lab announced and released Inkling 2 Mini on November 20, 2026. The coverage is a day later, so the release is not older than the sources imply.
kept.evidence: Source 0 is dated 'Nov 20, 2026' and says 'Today we are releasing Inkling 2 Mini'. Source 1 (dated Nov 21, 2026) says the lab 'announced the model on Friday'. Source 2 (Nov 21) says 'the release yesterday'.

kept.claim: Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer that runs the middle layers of the model three times for every token, so it can reason more while writing fewer tokens.
kept.evidence: Source 0: 'running the middle layers of the model three times for every token'. Source 1: 'runs its middle layers three times for every token'. Source 2: the 'middle 12 layers run three times using shared weights'.

kept.claim: The model is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 26.4B total parameters and 3.4B active parameters. Counting the loops, it uses 5.4B weight activations per token. It has 24 layers, giving 48 layer applications per token.
kept.evidence: Source 0: '26.4B total parameters, 3.4B active, and 5.4B weight activations per token to account for looping' and '48 layer applications per token from 24 stored layers'. Source 1 gives the same figures in 'bn'. Source 2 says '26.4 billion total parameters', '3.4 billion' active, '48 effective layer applications' and '5.4 billion effective active parameters'.

kept.claim: Total memory footprint is about 20GB, small enough to run on consumer laptops and desktop AI computers.
kept.evidence: Source 0: 'total memory footprint of Inkling 2 Mini is ~20GB'. Source 1: 'takes up about 20GB of memory'. Source 2: '~20GB memory footprint'.

kept.claim: Most weights were trained and deployed natively in 4-bit NVFP4. The last four layers are in 8-bit MXFP8, so there is no conversion loss from quantization.
kept.evidence: Source 0: 'trained and are deployed natively in NVFP4, with the last four layers in MXFP8'. Source 2: 'first 20 layers natively in 4-bit NVFP4 ... final four layers in 8-bit MXFP8'. Source 1 mentions only NVFP4.

kept.claim: Two-thirds of the experts were pruned during training, from 384 down to 128. The model was then trained on 1T tokens distilled from a larger internal Inkling model.
kept.evidence: Source 0: 'pruned two-thirds of the experts, leaving the 128 experts' and '1T tokens distilled from a larger internal Inkling model'. Source 1: 'cut two-thirds of the model's experts ... 1tn tokens'. Source 2: 'from 384 down to 128 ... 1 trillion tokens'.

kept.claim: Full weights are published openly on Hugging Face.
kept.evidence: Source 0: 'The full weights of Inkling 2 Mini ... are available on Hugging Face'. Source 1: 'The weights are on Hugging Face'. Source 2: 'released ... full weights on Hugging Face'.

kept.claim: The model is released under the Apache 2.0 license, paired with a Model Acceptable Use Policy. The primary announcement page I fetched does not state the license. I saw it on the model card only as a search snippet and did not fetch that page. Only the two press articles I fetched state it.
kept.evidence: Source 1: 'released under an Apache 2.0 licence'. Source 2: 'full weights on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license, paired with a standard Model Acceptable Use Policy'.

kept.claim: The model has a 1M-token (1 million) context window. The primary page I fetched does not state this.
kept.evidence: Source 1: 'context window of 1m tokens'. Source 2: 'across a 1-million-token context window'.

kept.claim: The model runs on laptops: at launch it is supported on any Mac (MacBook, Mac Mini) with at least 32GB RAM via Ollama. It also runs on NVIDIA DGX Spark.
kept.evidence: Source 0: 'any Mac system (MacBook, Mac Mini) with at least 32GB RAM via Ollama' and 'DGX Spark'. Source 1: 'runs through Ollama on Macs with at least 32GB of memory'. Source 2: 'offline on a 32GB MacBook Pro or a single desktop GPU' and lists '32GB+ Macs (Ollama, EXO), DGX Spark, 16GB+ via GGUF'.

kept.claim: Quantized GGUF versions are available via Unsloth and llama.cpp for local inference.
kept.evidence: Source 0: 'Quantized GGUF versions are available via Unsloth and llama.cpp'. Source 2 quotes Unsloth's GGUF builds with llama.cpp support and lists '16GB+ via GGUF'.

kept.claim: Thinking Machines reports Inkling 2 Mini leads every open-weights model with fewer than 100B total parameters on benchmarks such as DeepSWE v1.1, where it scores 48.2%.
kept.evidence: Source 0: 'leads every open-weights model with less than 100B total parameters on benchmarks such as DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%)'. Source 1: 'The lab reports 48.2% on DeepSWE v1.1'. Source 2: 'leads all sub-100B open-weights models on DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%)'.

kept.claim: Inkling 2 Mini scores 46.5% on Vals Index v2.2.
kept.evidence: Source 0: 'Vals Index v2.2 (46.5%)'. Source 2: 'Vals Index v2.2 (46.5%)'.

kept.claim: Inkling 2 Mini scores 77.9% on SWE-bench Pro v2 Hard.
kept.evidence: Source 0 benchmark table: 'SWEBench Pro v2 (Hard) ... 77.9%'. Source 1: '77.9% on a hard set of SWE-bench Pro tasks'. Source 2: 'SWE-bench Pro v2 Hard (77.9%)'.

kept.claim: Inkling 2 Mini scores 79.2% on SWE-bench Verified.
kept.evidence: Source 0 table: 'SWEBench Verified ... 79.2%'. Source 2: 'scoring 79.2% on SWE-bench Verified'.

kept.claim: Inkling 2 Mini scores 20.1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (v5.0), tying Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B. Source 1 rounds this to 20.
kept.evidence: Source 0 table: 'AA Index (v5.0) 20.1', the same as Qwen3.8-27B. Source 1: 'put Inkling 2 Mini at 20 on its Intelligence Index. That matches Qwen3.8 27B'. Source 2: 'both tie at 20.1'.

kept.claim: Artificial Analysis (a third-party tester, not fetched) reportedly found Inkling 2 Mini about six times cheaper and four times faster per task than Qwen3.8-27B. It cost $0.59 and took 9 minutes per task, against $3.53 and 38.2 minutes. The primary page I fetched does not state these figures.
kept.evidence: Source 1: 'Each task cost $0.59 and took nine minutes, against $3.53 and 38.2 minutes'. Source 2: 'runs four times faster (9.0 minutes per task versus 38.2 minutes), and costs six times less per task ($0.59 versus $3.53 at first-party API rates)'.

kept.claim: Qwen3.8-27B scored 42.2% on DeepSWE v1.1, against Inkling 2 Mini's 48.2%.
kept.evidence: Source 1: 'Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B scored 42.2%'. Source 2 table: 'Qwen3.8-27B ... 42.2%'.

kept.claim: The lab built an offline demo: researchers flew with the model, and on a MacBook Pro (M5 Pro, 48GB) in airplane mode it built a playable flight simulator in a few minutes.
kept.evidence: Source 0: 'it ran offline on a MacBook Pro and built a playable flight simulator in a few minutes'; the caption reads 'MacBook Pro (M5 Pro, 48GB) Airplane mode'. Source 1: 'built a playable flight simulator in a few minutes'. Source 2: 'a 48GB M5 Pro MacBook Pro to build a playable flight simulator in minutes'.

kept.claim: In a second demo, one offline MacBook ran all 20 villagers of a pixel town built by the model.
kept.evidence: Source 0: 'the same model powers all 20 villagers on one offline MacBook'. Source 1: 'a single offline MacBook ran all 20 villagers'. Source 2: 'powering 20 persistent autonomous villagers'.

kept.claim: In the lab's scaling test, a non-looping model cost 7.5% less compute to train but needed 140% more inference compute to match the looped model's loss on 512k-token agentic traces. Source 2 states only the 140% figure.
kept.evidence: Source 0: 'cost 7.5% less compute to train, but required 140% more inference compute ... on 512k-token agentic traces'. Source 1: 'cost 7.5% less to train, but needed 140% more compute at run time'. Source 2 gives only '140% more inference compute ... 512K-token agentic traces'.

kept.claim: Limitations: it is not the strongest small model for multi-turn chat or instructions with many constraints. It scores 50.0% on MultiChallenge and 33.4% on ComplexConstraints v1.1, behind Qwen3.8-27B on both. It also trails larger models on hard reasoning tests, and looping does not let the weights store more facts.
kept.evidence: Source 0: 'scores 50.0% on MultiChallenge and 33.4% on ComplexConstraints v1.1, behind Qwen3.8-27B on both'. Source 1 gives the same weaknesses without the percentages. Source 2 gives 50.0% and 33.4%, and notes factual recall scales with total parameter count.

kept.claim: Alongside Inkling 2 Mini, the lab released a research-specific variable-loop variant (TML-d24-varloop-research). Its no-CoT time horizon improved from 16 seconds at one pass to 37 seconds at three passes. Source 1 describes the model as looping one to five times.
kept.evidence: Source 0: 'research-specific variable-loop variant we are releasing alongside it' and 'improved from 16 seconds at one pass to 37 seconds with three'. Source 1: 'releasing a research model that can loop one to five' times. Source 2: 'companion variable-loop checkpoint ... trained for one to five passes' and '16 seconds ... 37 seconds'.

kept.claim: Stanford's intelligence-per-joule benchmark on an NVIDIA DGX Spark gave Inkling 2 Mini 0.703, against 0.430 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and 0.159 for Gemma-4-26B-A4B. The Gemma figure is read from source 2 only.
kept.evidence: Source 0: 'scored 0.703 running on NVIDIA DGX Spark ... 0.430 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B'. Source 2: 'scored 0.703, comfortably ahead of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (0.430) and Gemma-4-26B-A4B (0.159)'.

kept.claim: Thinking Machines Lab is Mira Murati's startup, and Murati is the former OpenAI CTO. This is background, not a claim of the primary announcement.
kept.evidence: Source 1: 'Mira Murati's startup'. Source 2: 'started and led by former OpenAI chief technology officer Mira Murati'.

dropped.claim: The model is multimodal: it accepts text and images as input and outputs text. The primary page I fetched does not state this.
dropped.evidence: Source 2: 'natively multimodal, accepting UTF-8 text and pixel-based images ... and outputting text'. Only one fetched source says this, so it is not double-confirmed.

dropped.claim: The model is available on Tinker for inference and fine-tuning, and in the Tinker Playground for chat. Only the primary source states this.
dropped.evidence: Source 0: 'available for inference and fine-tuning on Tinker, and for chat on the Tinker Playground'. Sources 1 and 2 do not say this about the release.

dropped.claim: Price: the weights are free to download under Apache 2.0, which source 2 describes as allowing royalty-free commercial use. Neither the primary page I fetched nor source 1 states a price for the weights. Hosted API pricing of $0.15 input / $0.50 output per 1M tokens (first-party), and from $0.08 / $0.35 on OpenRouter, appears only in source 2.
dropped.evidence: Source 2: 'royalty-free' under Apache 2.0, and a table listing '$0.15 / $0.50 (first-party); from $0.08 / $0.35 on OpenRouter'. Only one fetched source, so not double-confirmed.
